insider_note: Splitting (1+xlogx)/x into 1/x + logx before looking for f and f′ is the key move — the fraction as printed hides the pairing completely.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Split the fraction and identify f(x), f′(x)
steps.why: Dividing both terms of the numerator by x separates the bracket into 1/x and logx, which are exactly f′(x) and f(x) for f(x)=logx.
common_mistakes: Trying to spot f and f′ in the un-split fraction (1+xlogx)/x directly.
Splitting incorrectly as 1 + logx/x, losing the 1/x term.
steps.memory_tip: (1+xlogx)/x = 1/x + xlogx/x = 1/x + logx — divide EVERY term in the numerator by x separately.

steps.label: Apply the formula for the final answer
steps.why: With f(x)=logx identified, the standard eˣ[f+f′] result gives eˣlogx directly.
common_mistakes: Writing eˣ/x instead of eˣ logx in the final line.
steps.memory_tip: The answer keeps f(x)=logx, the term that survived after the split — not 1/x.
